segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we had come through safely, we then learned that the island was called Malta.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The natives showed us no ordinary kindness: they lit a fire and took us all in, because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man must certainly be a murderer. He came through the sea safely, but Justice has not allowed him to live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited expectantly for a long time and saw nothing unusual happening to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the neighborhood of that place there were estates belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It happened that Publius’s father was lying ill, suffering from bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses also came and were cured.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They also honored us with many honors, and when we were putting out to sea they supplied us with what we needed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered at the island, an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Gods as its figurehead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed three days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there we cast off and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where we found brothers and sisters and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The brothers and sisters there, having heard about us, came out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to live by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When they had examined me, they wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But when the Jews spoke against this, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any accusation to bring against my nation.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason, then, I have invited you here to see you and speak with you, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I wear this chain.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers come here and reported or said anything bad about you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we think it right to hear from you what your views are, for as to this sect, it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They set a day with him and came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning until evening he explained and testified to the kingdom of God, trying to persuade them about Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some were persuaded by what was said, but others would not believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Disagreeing with one another, they began to leave after Paul had said one thing:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your ancestors,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: saying, ‘Go to this people and say, “You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they have barely heard, and their eyes they have closed, so that they might never see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.”’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will indeed hear.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stayed two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, unhindered.

notes.note: The Greek word names people who did not speak Greek; the Maltese of this period spoke a Punic dialect. It carries no suggestion of savagery here, as the praise of their kindness shows, so “barbarians” would mislead. Most modern translations likewise use “natives” or “islanders.”

The islanders speak of Justice as a divine power that pursues the guilty, a familiar figure in Greek thought, where she was personified as a goddess. Their reasoning is that a man who escapes shipwreck only to be bitten by a snake must be a criminal whom divine retribution has caught. The capital letter reflects this personification, which most modern translations also recognize.

notes.phrase: the leading man of the island
notes.traditional: the chief man of the island
notes.note: The phrase is literally “the first man of the island.” It appears to be an official local title and not just a description of prominence; inscriptions from Malta are usually cited as attesting it. Whether Publius was the Roman governor’s representative or a native dignitary is not certain.

The Greek names the Dioscuri, the twin sons of Zeus, Castor and Pollux, who were regarded as protectors of sailors. Ships commonly carried a carved or painted emblem of a patron deity at the bow, which also served as the ship’s name.

notes.traditional: we fetched a compass, we made a circuit
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between a word meaning “taking away,” probably a nautical term for weighing anchor or casting off (compare its use with anchors in 27:40), and a similar-looking word meaning “going around,” that is, sailing a roundabout course. The SBLGNT prints the first, which is followed here, though its exact nautical sense is uncertain.

notes.phrase: the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns
notes.traditional: Appii Forum and The Three Taverns
notes.note: These were stopping places on the Appian Way, roughly forty and thirty miles south of Rome. Two groups of believers thus traveled a day or more out from the city to escort Paul in, the kind of reception customarily given to an honored visitor.

notes.phrase: Paul was permitted to live by himself
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add before this clause that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the camp; the words appear in the King James Version. The earliest witnesses lack them, and the SBLGNT does not include them.

This translation renders the verb “hand over” throughout, so that the reader can see the same word used of Jesus being handed over to the authorities and of Paul here. The phrasing echoes the prophecy of Agabus in 21:11 and the predictions of Jesus’s own suffering. Older versions have “delivered”; many modern ones already use “handed over” in this verse.

The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” in verse 28. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Israel; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. The translation follows the standard practice of dividing the two by sense.

The verse numbered 29 in older English Bibles (“And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the SBLGNT. It is generally regarded as a later addition, so the numbering passes from 28 to 30.

The Greek noun ordinarily means a price paid or rent, which gives “at his own expense.” Many translations instead take it as “in his own rented lodging,” which suits the verb “stayed” but is a sense not clearly attested for the word elsewhere. Either way the practical picture is the same: Paul lived in private quarters that he paid for, not in a prison.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (of believers generally); brothers (address to men, fellow Jews)
candidates.reason: The plural for the community recurs in nearly every book, and translations split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers,” so one policy by sense is needed.
Used in Acts for the Sadducees, Pharisees and the Jesus movement and in the letters for divisions; “sect,” “party,” “faction” and “heresy” compete and carry very different tones.
It recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians and Colossians, where “barbarian” misleads and “natives” does not fit, so the non-Greek-speaker sense needs one considered policy.
Very frequent across the Gospels, Acts and the letters; “preach” and “proclaim” are both common and the choice should not vary by chapter.
